stops.name: Beijing, Xiqin Quyi, eight songs for the emperor's eunuchs
stops.campa: Ricci writes Chinese lyrics, of moral rather than plainly Christian content, to accompany eight airs on the keyboard instrument he gave the emperor seven years before, publishing them as the Xiqin Quyi. The songs circulate well beyond the palace, reprinted in later Chinese anthologies of music and morals long after their author's name has faded from them; the instrument itself the eunuchs never quite master, but the words outlive the playing. By this year the mission counts some two thousand converts and four residences across the empire, the slow harvest of the disguise, the geometry and the friendship all sown at once.

stops.name: Beijing, the memoirs begun
stops.campa: In what will prove his last full year, Ricci begins setting down in Italian the long history of the mission from Macau to Peking, a memoir candid about failures and reversals as much as successes, meant as instruction for the Jesuits who will carry the work on after him. He does not finish polishing it; it will be found among his papers, carried to Europe, and expanded by Nicolas Trigault into the printed history that first tells the whole of this journey, Zhaoqing's expulsion, Shaozhou's robbers, the shut gate at Peking, to a European readership that has never heard any of it.

stops.name: Beijing, the death of the Master from the West
stops.campa: Ricci falls seriously ill in the spring and, sensing the end, commends the mission to his brethren and to Xu Guangqi's continued protection at court. He closes his eyes as if turning some last matter over in thought, and dies quietly in his room beside the small Peking church, fifty-seven years old, twenty-eight of them spent inside China and never once returned to Italy. Word of his death runs through the capital's scholarly circles with real grief; converts and curious mandarins alike come to the house to see the body of the Sage of the Great West laid out.

stops.name: Beijing, the petition for a grave inside the Middle Kingdom
stops.campa: By Ming law and custom a foreigner who dies in the empire is carried home or laid outside the walls among the unclaimed. Diego de Pantoja, Ricci's companion of the tribute road, petitions the throne instead for ground inside the capital itself, an honor never before granted a Westerner, pleading the dead man's twenty-eight years in China and his standing among the empire's own scholars. Xu Guangqi and the mission's mandarin friends press the memorial forward through the Ministry of Rites. It is a bold request, and by every precedent unlikely to succeed.

stops.name: Beijing, the ground beyond Fuchengmen granted
stops.campa: The Wanli Emperor, who received Ricci's clocks and instruments for nine years without ever once receiving the man, grants the petition: a garden and villa beyond the Fuchengmen gate, lately confiscated from a disgraced eunuch, are made over to the Jesuits as a burial ground. The exact day of the edict is not preserved. The ground is handed across in the winter, and through the months following the fathers convert the eunuch's pavilion into a chapel fit to receive the coffin. It is the first earth in China a Western Christian will ever legally hold.

stops.name: Beijing, the funeral procession from Xuanwumen
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of April the funeral leaves the Jesuit house at Xuanwumen, where Ricci died, and crosses the capital westward to the granted ground: a Christian rite carried openly through Peking, mandarins and converts walking behind the coffin of a foreigner the emperor's own edict has honored. Nothing like it has been seen in the Ming capital. The coffin is set in the chapel raised inside the confiscated garden and left there while the vault is finished, and the city's scholars come out to read the tablet naming Li Madou, the Master from the Great West.

stops.name: Beijing, laid in the earth at Zhalan
stops.campa: In November, after months in the chapel, Ricci's coffin is lowered at last into the ground beyond Fuchengmen, the plot that will grow into the Zhalan Cemetery, first and eldest of the burial grounds Peking will keep for three centuries of missionaries after him. His epitaph, carved at the court's own sufferance, names him teacher and friend to China as much as priest. Xu Guangqi outlives him by more than twenty years, rising to Grand Secretary and shielding the mission Ricci built, one disguise, one map, one geometry, one friendship at a time, from Zhaoqing's shut door to the emperor's own confiscated garden.
